passage: In Kumasi, sixteen-year-old Kwame got the top mark in his class on a maths test, and he had written it with a chewed blue pen he'd found on the bus. After that, the blue pen came to every test. Physics: a good mark. History: good. Kwame kept it in a separate pocket, wrapped in a tissue. The night before chemistry, the pen ran dry. He shook it, breathed on it, scribbled on his palm. Nothing. His younger sister Rania watched from the doorway. "You studied, right?" "Yes, but the pen..." "The pen didn't study." She tossed him a black one. Kwame turned it over in his fingers, uneasy. Next day his hand shook a little on the first question. Then he remembered the formulas, and it steadied.

qa.q: Where had Kwame found the blue pen?
qa.a: On the bus.

qa.q: Why did Kwame feel uneasy holding the black pen?
qa.a: He had linked his good marks to the blue pen, so writing without it felt like losing his luck, even though he had studied.

qa.q: What turning point showed Kwame what really carried him in the chemistry test?
qa.a: When he remembered the formulas and his hand steadied: the studying, not the pen, was doing the work.

qa.q: How does Rania see Kwame's panic over the pen?
qa.a: Rania seems to find it a little silly and reminds him that "the pen didn't study"; the credit belongs to Kwame's own work.

grounding: A teenage boy credits a lucky pen for his marks and panics when it runs dry, reading cause into coincidence.

passage: At the badminton club, everyone knew about Vandana's socks: yellow, with a hole at the left toe. I'm going to lose." Coach Madhuri didn't laugh. She opened the scorebook. "Let's look. Five matches in those socks since March. Three wins, two losses. And two wins in other socks." Vandana frowned at the page. "But the first win..." "Was the week you practised your smash every evening," said Madhuri. Vandana looked down at her plain white socks. She still felt jittery walking on court. But she remembered the smash.

Dear Sharmila,
You'll laugh, but I have to confess my table-tennis madness. Remember the orange wristband you gave me before you moved? I wore it for the zonal match in July and won 3–0. Since then it's come to every single match. Six wins. I stopped washing it on match weeks, which Mummy says is a crime against the house, and Papa now calls me his superstitious daughter.
Here's the weird part. Last Saturday, in the final, I got to the hall and realised I'd left it on my bed. I nearly cried. I actually played the first game thinking, it's over. And then I won. 3–1.
Now I don't know what to believe. Was it ever the wristband? Or was it all the practice?
I'm still wearing it tomorrow, though. Just in case.
Mahima

qa.q: What score did Mahima win the final by?
qa.a: She won 3–1.

qa.q: What was Mahima thinking when she realised the wristband was at home?
qa.a: She felt scared and hopeless, nearly crying, because she had linked the wristband with her six wins and believed she would lose.

qa.q: What turning point could help Mahima see what really caused her wins?
qa.a: Winning the final without the wristband; she could compare that with her practice hours and see the wins came from her play.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel reading that her gift became a lucky charm?
qa.a: Sharmila might be touched and amused, and perhaps want to remind Mahima that the wins were her own.

grounding: A teen wears the same wristband to every match after one win, reading a link between it and results.

passage: Shreya, you asked me, Manjula, about my chess shirt, so here's the story. It's grey, with an ink stain on the pocket. I wore it the day I beat the state junior champion, at fifteen, and after that I was sure it was lucky. I wore it to every match for a year. My mother would find it drying on the balcony at midnight. When I lost, I told myself I'd played badly despite the shirt. When I won, it was the shirt. See how that works? Then my coach asked me to keep a proper scorebook. Every match, what I wore, the result. By December it said: six wins in the shirt, five losses in the shirt. Two wins in my school uniform. I sat there with that little book and felt silly. The shirt wasn't doing anything. It just happened to be there when I was good.

qa.q: What did the scorebook show about matches in the grey shirt?
qa.a: Six wins and five losses in the shirt.

qa.q: Why did Manjula feel silly sitting with the scorebook?
qa.a: Because the numbers showed the shirt made no difference, though Manjula had been certain it did.

qa.q: What choice helped Manjula see the truth, and why does it work?
qa.a: Keeping a scorebook of every match, not just the memorable wins, showed coincidence rather than cause.

qa.q: How might Manjula's mother have seen the midnight shirt drying?
qa.a: She probably found it a bit tiring but also sweet, a sign of how much the matches mattered.

grounding: A teen wears the same shirt to every match after one big win, taking coincidence for cause.

passage:
In the small town of Kotputli, the school volleyball court was mostly dust and a sagging net. Minakshi, fifteen, tied the same faded green ribbon in her hair before every match. She had worn it the day they beat the district team in March.
"Ribbon," she reminded herself, tightening it before Saturday's game.
They lost, badly.
On the bus home, Leela sat beside her. "So, the ribbon?"
Minakshi frowned. "It must be loose. I tied it wrong."
"Or," said Leela, "we won in March because Sunita was serving, and today she's got the flu."
Minakshi looked out at the mustard fields. She knew that. She did. But the ribbon felt safer to blame than to lose.
She untied it and held it in her fist the whole way home.

qa.q: Who was serving when they beat the district team in March, according to Leela?
qa.a: Sunita was serving.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi hold the ribbon in her fist all the way home?
qa.a: She felt torn and a little uneasy, knowing Leela was right but still wanting to believe the ribbon mattered.

qa.q: What would you advise Minakshi about the ribbon?
qa.a: She can keep it if it calms her, but she should look at real reasons like who is playing and how they practise when judging wins and losses.

qa.q: How does Leela see Minakshi's ribbon?
qa.a: Leela sees it as a coincidence and points to the real cause, the team's best server being sick.

grounding: It shows a teenager treating a ribbon as the cause of a win, reading a link into coincidence.
